How to use this primer

This booklet teaches petroleum and natural gas processing from zero, in the order the exam needs it. Read it once before the Complete Solutions. Each section has a green core idea box (learn this first), the key figure, the formulas with every symbol and unit, and a short worked example. Most of this course is descriptive: you score by drawing the process diagram and explaining each step in order. The numericals are few and repeat every year (API, viscosity blending, VI, gas properties, Campbell water content, separator sizing, Darcy flow), so they are easy marks once you know the steps.

The pass set (from the Question Map): refining A1-A7 and natural gas B1-B6; B7 (Darcy flow and orifice meter) is the next to add. Question numbers move (in 2021 the two sections were swapped), so learn by topic.

The whole course on one page

Read the map as two parallel factories. The refinery (Section A) takes liquid crude oil, separates it by boiling point, converts the heavy and low-octane parts into valuable fuels, cleans out sulfur and blends the products. The gas plant (Section B) takes the gas stream from the well, separates liquids, removes water and acid gases, and either pipes the gas or liquefies it (LNG, LPG (liquefied petroleum gas)).

Units and maths refresher

The oil and gas industry uses field units: pressure in psi, temperature in °F or °R, volume in barrels and cubic feet, flow in bbl/day or MMscfd. Learn the conversions once and write the unit on every line.

QuantityConversion / rule
absolute temperature°R = °F + 460 (459.67); K = °C + 273.15; °F = 1.8°C + 32
absolute pressurepsia = psig + 14.7; 1 atm = 14.696 psi = 101.325 kPa = 760 mmHg
volume1 bbl (barrel) = 42 US gal = 5.615 ft3 = 0.159 m3; 1 m3 = 35.31 ft3 = 6.29 bbl
gas volumescf = standard cubic foot at 14.7 psia and 60 °F; MMscf = 106 scf; MMscfd = 106 scf per day
area1 acre = 43,560 ft2
densityρ = SG × 1000 kg/m3 = SG × 62.4 lbm/ft3
viscosity1 cP = 10−3 Pa·s; kinematic 1 cSt = 1 mm2/s; ν = μ/ρ
permeability1 darcy = 1000 md (millidarcy) ≈ 0.987 × 10−12 m2

Logarithms (needed for blending and radial flow)

  • log10 100 = 2 because 102 = 100; to undo a log, raise 10 to it: if log ν = 2.0997 then ν = 102.0997 = 125.8.
  • ln (natural log) uses base e = 2.718: ln(r/rw) grows slowly, so pressure changes fast near the well and slowly far away.
  • Powers: 121.25 = 22.3 (calculator: 12 ^ 1.25); to undo x1.25, raise to 1/1.25 = 0.8.

Mole-fraction averages (Kay’s rule)

For a gas mixture, a property of the mixture is often estimated as Σ yiPi, where yi is the mole fraction (mol% ÷ 100). Make a table with columns y, M, pc, Tc and the three products; sum each product column. Check that the y column adds to 1.000.

Crude oil and hydrocarbons (A1)

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons (only C and H) of many sizes and shapes, plus small amounts of S, N, O, metals, salt and water. Size decides boiling point (bigger = higher boiling). Shape decides quality: branched chains and benzene rings resist engine knock; straight chains ignite easily (good for diesel, bad for petrol).

FamilyGeneral formulaSaturated?Key quality
Paraffin (alkane)CnH2n+2yes (all single bonds)n-paraffins: high cetane, low octane; iso-paraffins: high octane
Naphthene (cycloalkane)CnH2nyes, ringmedium octane; turned into aromatics by reforming
AromaticCnH2n−6 (benzene ring)no (ring with alternating double bonds)very high octane; low cetane; smoke
Olefin (alkene)CnH2nno, C=Cmade by cracking; high octane but unstable (gum)

API gravity measures how light an oil is:

API = 141.5/SG − 131.5

SymbolMeaningUnit
SGspecific gravity of the oil at 60 °F (density ÷ density of water)–
APIAmerican Petroleum Institute gravity (water = 10)°API

Example: SG 0.85 → 141.5/0.85 = 166.47 → API = 35.0 (a light/medium crude). Lighter oil = higher API = more gasoline = more valuable.

Fuel quality numbers (A2)

A petrol (spark-ignition) engine needs fuel that does not self-ignite when compressed: high octane number. A diesel (compression-ignition) engine needs fuel that does self-ignite quickly: high cetane number. Volatility is measured by distillation, RVP (Reid vapour pressure) and flash point.

NumberReference fuels (100 / 0)High value means
Octane (RON, MON (motor octane number))iso-octane / n-heptaneresists knock; allows higher compression ratio
Cetanen-cetane (C16H34) / α-methylnaphthaleneshort ignition delay; smooth diesel combustion
RVP (psi)–evaporates easily: easy cold start, but vapour lock and losses if too high
Flash point (°C)–safer to store (needs higher temperature to flash)

Separating crude: distillation and desalting (A3)

Distillation separates by boiling point. The crude is first desalted (washed with water, then the water is removed in an electric field), heated in a furnace, and flashed into the atmospheric column. The heavy residue that would crack if heated further is distilled in a vacuum column, where low pressure lowers boiling points.

Stokes’ law explains settling in the desalter:

v = g d2(ρw − ρo)/(18μo)

SymbolMeaningUnit
vsettling velocity of a water dropm/s
ddrop diameterm
ρw, ρodensity of water and oilkg/m3
μooil viscosityPa·s

So the desalter makes drops bigger (electric field, d2) and the oil thinner (heating lowers μ): both raise v.

Changing molecules: reforming, isomerization, cracking (A4, A5)

Reforming rearranges naphtha molecules into aromatics (octane up, H2 released) over a platinum catalyst; reactions absorb heat, so the gas is reheated between reactors. Isomerization turns straight C5/C6 chains into branched ones. Cracking breaks big molecules into small ones: thermally (coking, visbreaking) or with a catalyst (FCC) or with catalyst + hydrogen (hydrocracking).

Endothermic = absorbs heat (temperature falls through the bed); exothermic = releases heat. A bifunctional catalyst has a metal site (Pt: adds/removes hydrogen) and an acid site (alumina, zeolite: rearranges and breaks carbon chains).

Cleaning with hydrogen and making lube oil (A6)

Hydrotreating: hydrogen over a Co-Mo or Ni-Mo catalyst turns sulfur into H2S and nitrogen into NH3, which are washed out; the fuel is left clean and stable. Lube oil is made by removing asphalt, aromatics and wax from vacuum distillates, then polishing with hydrogen.

Blending and viscosity index (A7)

Some properties mix like an average (SG, sulfur). Others do not (viscosity, RVP, flash point). For those, convert each component to a blending index, average the indices by volume fraction, then convert back.

xi = Vi/ΣV; BIvis = logν/(3 + logν); νblend = 103BI/(1−BI); BIRVP = RVP1.25; VI = 100(L − U)/(L − H)

SymbolMeaningUnit
xivolume fraction of component i–
νkinematic viscositycSt
RVPReid vapour pressurepsi
Uviscosity of the test oil at 40 °CcSt
L, H40 °C viscosity of VI-0 and VI-100 reference oils with the same 100 °C viscosity as the test oilcSt

Example: equal volumes of 50 cSt and 200 cSt oil. BI = 1.699/4.699 = 0.3616 and 2.301/5.301 = 0.4341; average 0.3978; logν = 3 × 0.3978/0.6022 = 1.982; ν = 95.9 cSt (not the simple average 125).

Natural gas basics and the phase envelope (B1)

Natural gas is mainly methane. Wet gas carries heavier components that condense to condensate when cooled. The phase envelope (p-T diagram) shows where a mixture is liquid, gas or both; gas-condensate reservoirs lie between the critical point and the cricondentherm, where lowering pressure makes liquid (retrograde condensation).

Real gas properties (B2)

Real gas: pV = znRT. z is read from the Standing-Katz chart using pseudo-reduced pressure and temperature (p/ppc, T/Tpc), where ppc, Tpc are mole-fraction averages of the critical constants. Sour gas needs the Wichert-Aziz correction.

ρg = pMa/(zRT); Bg = 0.02827 zT/p; γg = Ma/28.97; cg = 1/p − (1/z)(dz/dp)

SymbolMeaningUnit
pabsolute pressurepsia
Tabsolute temperature°R
zgas compressibility (deviation) factor–
Maapparent molecular weight ΣyiMilb/lb-mol
Rgas constant 10.73psia·ft3/(lb-mol·°R)
Bggas formation volume factorft3/scf
cgisothermal gas compressibilitypsi−1
φporosityfraction
kpermeabilitymd

Example: methane (M = 16.04) at 1000 psia, 100 °F (560 °R), z = 0.89: ρ = 1000 × 16.04/(0.89 × 10.73 × 560) = 3.00 lbm/ft3; Bg = 0.02827 × 0.89 × 560/1000 = 0.0141 ft3/scf.

Separators (B3)

A separator slows the well stream down (inlet diverter), gives droplets time to fall (settling section), catches fine mist (mist extractor) and holds liquid long enough for gas to escape (liquid section). Size it for gas (diameter, Souders-Brown) and for liquid (retention volume), and take the larger.

D2 = qgZ(T + 460)ρg0.5/[2.40Kp(ρL − ρg)0.5]; VL = Wt/1440; VL = 0.1399D2h (vertical)

SymbolMeaningUnit
Dseparator diameterft
qggas rateMMscfd
Ttemperature°F
KSouders-Brown constant (0.167 vertical, 0.382 horizontal, 0.35 sphere)–
Wliquid rate = GLR (gas-liquid ratio) × qgbbl/day
tretention timemin
VLliquid settling volumebbl

Water, hydrates and dehydration (B4)

Gas from the well is saturated with water. If it cools under pressure, liquid water and gas form hydrates (solid). Remove the water with glycol (absorption) or solid desiccants (adsorption); or keep the gas warm, lower the pressure, or inject methanol/glycol.

Campbell water content of a sour gas: W = yHCWHC + yCO2WCO2 + yH2SWH2S, each W read from its chart at the gas p and T (lb water per MMscf).

Sweetening (B5)

H2S (toxic, corrosive) and CO2 (no heat value, freezes, corrosive) are removed by a liquid that reacts with them when cold and at high pressure and releases them when hot and at low pressure (amine), or by a solid that reacts with them (iron sponge for small H2S).

LNG (liquefied natural gas) and LPG (B6)

LNG: methane cooled to −162 °C, 600 times smaller, shipped in insulated double-hull tankers. Before cooling, everything that could freeze (CO2, water, heavy hydrocarbons) and mercury are removed. LPG: propane + butane, liquid under small pressure, sold in cylinders; heavier than air, so leaks collect at floor level.

Flow through rock and gas meters (B7)

Darcy’s law: flow through rock is proportional to permeability, area and pressure drop, and inversely proportional to viscosity and length. Around a well the flow is radial and pressure rises with ln r: most of the pressure is lost near the well.

q = 0.001127 kA(p1 − p2)/(μL); p = pwf + [qBμ/(0.00708kh)] ln(r/rw)

SymbolMeaningUnit
qflow ratebbl/day
kpermeabilitymd
Across-section areaft2
μviscositycp
Llengthft
hreservoir thicknessft
Boil formation volume factorbbl/STB
rwwell radiusft

Example: k = 50 md, A = 1000 ft2, Δp = 100 psi, μ = 1 cp, L = 500 ft: q = 0.001127 × 50 × 1000 × 100/(1 × 500) = 11.3 bbl/day.
